REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS

             Pursuant to Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 3131 and Rule 7132 of the Rules of Practice

and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), the

Indicated PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) Transmission Owners (“Indicated TOs”)3 request

rehearing of the Commission’s order in the above-captioned dockets.4 The Commission’s 206

Order is arbitrary and capricious and not based upon reasoned decision making.                                  The

Commission’s directive for changes to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”)

exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction and is not permitted under the FPA.

          Before turning to the problems with the Commission’s decision to impose new Contract

Demand Network Service (“CD Service”)5 and a new interim non-firm transmission service

(“Interim Service”), the Indicated TOs wish to express their support for certain helpful

clarifications in the 206 Order: (1) An Eligible Customer6 serving a co-located load must be

designated because it is the Eligible Customer that seeks and obtains transmission service and pays

for it;7 (2) Transmission service to co-located loads must be metered (apart from metering of any

retail energy sales or distribution services);8 (3) Existing Network Integration Transmission

Service (“NITS” or “Network Service”) should be based on Gross Load; 9 and (4) Behind the Meter

Generation (“BTMG”) provisions do not apply to co-located loads or provide a basis to take

transmission service on a basis other than gross load.10




5

6
     An “Eligible Customer” is defined in the PJM Tariff to mean the following:

         (i) Any electric utility (including any Transmission Owner and any power marketer), Federal power
             marketing agency, or any person generating electric energy for sale for resale is an Eligible
             Customer under the Tariff. Electric energy sold or produced by such entity may be electric
             energy produced in the United States, Canada or Mexico. However, with respect to transmission
             service that the Commission is prohibited from ordering by Section 212(h) of the Federal Power
             Act, such entity is eligible only if the service is provided pursuant to a state requirement that the
             Transmission Provider or Transmission Owner offer the unbundled transmission service, or
             pursuant to a voluntary offer of such service by a Transmission Owner.

         (ii) Any retail customer taking unbundled transmission service pursuant to a state requirement that
             the Transmission Provider or a Transmission Owner offer the transmission service, or pursuant
             to a voluntary offer of such service by a Transmission Owner, is an Eligible Customer under the
             Tariff. As used in Tariff, Part VI, Eligible Customer shall mean only those Eligible Customers
             that have submitted a Completed Application.

          These clarifications should sufficiently answer the relevant questions presented by this

proceeding. While the Indicated TOs appreciate the Commission’s leadership in addressing this

issue, the 206 Order goes beyond these clarifications and attempts to fix something that is not

broken. There are indeed issues requiring attention in the PJM wholesale markets—including

resource adequacy, reliability, and affordability challenges for reasons other than transmission

service offerings and rates—but the creation of new forms of transmission service does not address

those challenges and instead risks making those very real problems worse.

         “The reasonableness of a rate is assessed in light of the FPA’s goals of promoting reliable

service at reasonable rates and developing plentiful energy supplies.”11 The existing transmission

services under the existing PJM Tariff are consistent with those goals and are just and reasonable.

No one has satisfied the burden under FPA section 20612 to demonstrate that the existing tariff is

unjust and unreasonable. Nor has the burden been satisfied to demonstrate that the Commission’s

replacement rate is just and reasonable. The Commission’s replacement rate that imposes new CD

Service and Interim Service options could directly place at risk the reliability of PJM’s electric

grid and grant an undue preference to certain categories of customers. The new services could

allow co-located load to pay for a different share of transmission system embedded costs than other

customers, thereby resulting in rates that are not just and reasonable.

         It appears that the primary driver of the Commission’s ruling was a desire to speed service

to certain customers—those who are co-located with generators.13 The Indicated TOs support the

desire to allow prompt service to all customers at locations that make efficient use of the existing



11
     Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1035 (D.C. Cir. 2022).
12
     16 U.S.C. § 824e.
13

                                                         3
 system, but the CD Service and Interim Service do nothing to advance those goals. Instead, the

new services are premised on the fiction that a customer taking CD Service or Interim Service

imposes different burdens on the grid than customers taking traditional network service. From this

false premise the Commission draws two conclusions. First, the Commission concludes that,

because co-located loads impose fewer burdens on the system, such facilities, and especially co-

located load facilities combined with system protection commitments, should be encouraged

through special incentives to minimize the need for system upgrades. As demonstrated later

herein, new load already has powerful incentives to site their facilities and utilize protective

equipment to minimize the need for system upgrades and to avoid the delays attendant to system

upgrades. But the question of whether new transmission upgrades are needed to accommodate a

new load must be based on engineering and technical data, such as the extent of the load, its

operating characteristics, and how the system will react under various scenarios to changes in the

load. Such studies will not be based simply on theoretical net load regardless of whether imperfect

protective systems are in place.

       The false presumption that co-located facilities impose reduced burdens on the system

drives a second Commission assumption that co-located loads should pay lower rates than other

users. This proposition violates a long-held Commission policy that all users of the transmission

network should pay the same load-ratio share of network cost, regardless of claims that some users

impose different burdens on the system. As demonstrated herein, the demands on the system of

co-located loads are material and no less significant than the burdens on the system of other

transmission users whose demands for special rates consistently have been rejected. Placing the

meter for the load at a different location, or establishing a contractual arrangement for service

thereto, does nothing to alter the physics of operating the system. As explained in detail later, co-



                                                 4
 located loads derive significant operational and financial benefits from being interconnected with

the grid. These benefits significantly outweigh the cost of paying full network service rates.

       There has been no demonstration that the existing rate is not just and reasonable, and the

Commission has not demonstrated that any replacement rate is anything other than arbitrary and

capricious. The Commission should therefore reverse its decision and reaffirm that the existing

PJM tariff is just and reasonable.

       I.      Statement of Issues/Specification of Error.

       In accordance with 18 C.F.R. § 385.713(c)(1) and (2), the Indicated TOs provide the

following specification of errors and statement of issues, including citations to representative

Commission and judicial precedent.

            1. The Burden Under FPA Section 206 Has Not Been Met: The Existing Rate Has
               Not Been Shown to Be Unjust and Unreasonable. See 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a); Pub.
               Citizen, Inc. v. FERC, 7 F.4th 1177, 1183 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (explaining that “[t]he
               burden of proving” that a rate is unjust or unreasonably is placed on “the party that
               initiated the proceeding”).

                   a. There is No Evidence In the Record That Co-Located Loads Are
                      Unable to Obtain Reliable, Timely, and Reasonably Priced Service
                      Using the Existing Network Service Construct. Therefore, the
                      Commission Fails To Satisfy the Requirement Under the
                      Administrative Procedure Act That Its Decision Be Supported With
                      Substantial Evidence.

                           i. The Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”) requires the
                              Commission to “examine the relevant data and articulate a
                              satisfactory explanation for its action including a ‘rational
                              connection between the facts found and the choice made,’” and
                              to base its decision on substantial evidence; because FERC has
                              failed to do so, its decision is arbitrary and capricious. Motor
                              Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. (“State
                              Farm”), 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (citation omitted); see Fla. Gas
                              Transmission Co. v. FERC (“Florida Gas”), 604 F.3d 636, 639
                              (D.C. Cir. 2010) (“[T]he Commission ‘must be able to demonstrate
                              that it has made a reasoned decision based upon substantial evidence
                              in the record.’”) (citation omitted); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y. v.
                              NLRB, 305 U.S. 197, 229 (1938) (explaining that substantial

     evidence means “more than a mere scintilla”); see also 5 U.S.C.
    § 706.

ii. The PJM Tariff provides two transmission service options
    (Network Integration Transmission Service and Point-to-Point
    Transmission Service) and includes provisions to explain how
    those services work and how Network Customers will be Served.
    See PJM Tariff at §§ 31.1, 31.2, 31.3, 31.6 and 32; see also generally
    PJM Tariff , OATT Definitions.

iii. To the extent that parties have argued they are unable to

     https://ir.talenenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-

     See also Exelon Dec. 8, 2025 Comments at 6.

iv. Ignoring data in the record regarding the ability of co-located
    load to interconnect to the transmission system violates the APA
    and renders FERC’s decision arbitrary and capricious. See
    State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

v. There is no evidence in the record that the cost of Network
   Service impacts the development of data centers. Nor is there
   evidence to support that Network Service imposes unnecessary
   upgrades on all customers. Nor is there evidence that new forms
   of transmission service will allow for faster interconnection. See
   Florida Gas, 604 F.3d at 639 (“[T]he Commission ‘must be able to
   demonstrate that it has made a reasoned decision based upon
   substantial evidence in the record.’”) (citation omitted); Consol.
   Edison Co. of N.Y., 305 U.S. at 229 (explaining that substantial
   evidence means “more than a mere scintilla”); see also 5 U.S.C.
   § 706.

vi. The Commission has not met its burden under FPA section 206
    because it acknowledges that the existing transmission services

           ¶ 61,217 at P 195 (finding Network Service charged on a gross
           demand basis to be “one just and reasonable transmission service
           option”).

b. The Commission Did Not Engage in Reasoned Decision Making
   Because It Did Not Explain its Departure from FERC Precedent or
   Refute that, Because the Existing PJM Tariff Provides Service on the
   Same Basis for All Customers, the Existing PJM Tariff Does Not Grant
   an Undue Preference. See F.C.C. v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556
   U.S. 502, 515 (2009) (“[T]he requirement that an agency provide reasoned
   explanation for its action would ordinarily demand that it display awareness
   that it is changing position. An agency may not, for example, depart from
   a prior policy sub silentio or simply disregard rules that are still on the
   books.”); New England Power Generators Ass’n v. FERC, 881 F.3d 202,
   211 (D.C. Cir. 2018) (“Although case-by-case adjudication sometimes
   results in decisions that seem at odds but can be distinguished on their facts,
   it is the agency’s responsibility to provide a reasoned explanation of why
   those facts matter.”); W. Deptford Energy, LLC v. FERC, 766 F.3d 10, 20
   (D.C. Cir. 2014) (“It is textbook administrative law that an agency must
   ‘provide[ ] a reasoned explanation for departing from precedent or treating
   similar situations differently,’ and Commission cases are no exception.”)
   (citations omitted); Cal. Pub. Utils. Comm’n v. FERC, 879 F.3d 966, 977
   (9th Cir. 2018) (“FERC departed from this policy without acknowledgment
   or explanation. This departure was arbitrary and capricious.”); Sw. Airlines
   Co. v. FERC, 926 F.3d 851, 856 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (“‘A full and rational
   explanation’ becomes ‘especially important’ when, as here, an agency
   elects to ‘shift [its] policy’ or ‘depart[ ] from its typical manner of’
   administering a program. . . . [FERC] must at least ‘acknowledge’ its
   seemingly inconsistent precedents and either offer a reason ‘to distinguish
   them’ or ‘explain its apparent rejection of their approach’ . . . . But however
   the agency justifies its new position, what it may not do is ‘gloss[ ] over or
   swerve[ ] from prior precedents without discussion.’”) (most alterations in
   original) (citations omitted); see also 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b) (prohibiting a
   public utility from making or granting an “undue preference or advantage”
   or from maintaining “any unreasonable difference in rates, charges, service,
   facilities, or in any other respect, . . . as between classes of service”);
   TransCanada Power Mktg. Ltd. v. FERC, 811 F.3d 1, 12–13 (D.C. Cir.
   2015) (remanding because FERC did not adequately explain its position).

        i. The Commission has a long-standing policy of rejecting
           attempts by network transmission customers to avoid paying
           their load ratio share of system cost. See, e.g., Nat’l R.R.
           Passenger Corp. v. PPL Elec. Utils. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,237 at

       c. The Loads Rely Upon the Entire Embedded Transmission System to
          Serve Their Full Gross Load. Therefore, FERC’s Decision is Arbitrary
          and Capricious Because the Embedded Transmission System Costs
          Should Be Charged For Those Transmission Services. See Decl. of
          David Weaver, PE, Attachment 1 to Exelon Comments, Docket No. EL25-

               i. The Commission’s failure to consider the benefits of grid
                  interconnection makes the 206 Order arbitrary and capricious.
                  See State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

              ii. The Commission’s 206 Order is arbitrary and capricious
                  because it failed to consider the unique issues that attend co-
                  location with nuclear plants. See id.; Decl. of David Weaver, PE,
                  Attachment 1 to Exelon Comments, Docket No. EL25-20 (Dec. 12,

2. The Burden Has Not Been Met Under FPA Section 206: FERC’s Replacement
   Rate is Not Just and Reasonable. See 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a); Advanced Energy
   Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 663 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (“If the Commission finds
   that a rate is ‘unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential, the
   Commission shall determine the just and reasonable rate ... and shall fix the same
   by order,’” and “[i]t is the Commission’s job—not the petitioner’s—to find a just

                                    8
 and reasonable rate.”) (alterations in original) (citation omitted); Emera Maine v.
FERC, 854 F.3d 9, 21 (D.C. Cir. 2017); Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1,
10 (D.C. Cir. 2002). The 206 Order failed to address the fact that reliability is
relevant to the inquiry of whether a rate is just and reasonable. See
Constellation Mystic Power, LLC v. FERC, 45 F.4th 1028, 1035 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
(“The reasonableness of a rate is assessed in light of the FPA’s goals of promoting
reliable service at reasonable rates and developing plentiful energy supplies.”);
NAACP v. FPC, 425 U.S. 662, 669–70 (1976) (“[T]he principal purpose of [the
FPA is] to encourage the orderly development of plentiful supplies of electricity
. . . at reasonable prices.”).

   a. Allowing Special Treatment For Co-Located Load Violates the FPA’s
      Requirement That There Be No Undue Preference Or Unreasonable
      Difference In Rates Between Classes of Service. See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b).

           i. To the extent that the Commission suggests that the
              transmission provider may move forward with interconnection
              before studies are completed, such course of action would
              jeopardize reliability and would be in tension with NERC
              reliability standards. See, e.g., See NERC, FAC-002-4 – Facility
              Interconnection                                            Studies
              (2022), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/standards/reliability-
              standards/fac/fac-002-4.pdf; NERC, 181 FERC ¶ 61,126 (2022)
              (approving FAC-002-4).

           ii. There is no lawful basis to require tariff changes to impose new
               forms of service that give certain customers a reduced share of
               embedded costs compared to all other users when they receive
               the same benefits. See Coal. of MISO Transmission Customers v.
               FERC, 45 F.4th 1004, 1009 (D.C. Cir. 2022).

   b. The Commission’s Emphasis on Protective Systems Is In Tension With
      the Commission’s Open Access Policies and Therefore Is Arbitrary and
      Capricious. The Commission Also Erred In Minimizing the Fact that
      Protective Systems Can and Have Failed. See NERC, Characteristics
      and Risks of Emerging Large Loads: Large Loads Task Force White Paper,
      at 13 (July 2025), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-
      are/standing-committees/rstc/whitepaper-characteristics-and-risks-of-
      emerging-large-loads.pdf.

           i. The Commission erred in adopting a policy in tension with its
              open access policies. See Promoting Wholesale Competition
              Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission Services
              by Public Utilities; Recovery of Stranded Costs by Public Utilities
              and Transmitting Utilities, Order No. 888-A, FERC Stats. & Regs.
              ¶ 31,048, 62 Fed. Reg. 12,274 (Mar. 14, 1997), order on reh’g,
              Order No. 888-B, 81 FERC ¶ 61,248 (1997), order on reh’g, Order

           nom. Transmission Access Pol’y Study Grp. v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667
           (D.C. Cir. 2000), aff’d sub nom. New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1
           (2002).

c. The 206 Order is Arbitrary and Capricious in Abandoning the Main
   Construct of Service to Load, Which is That Customers Share In the
   Embedded Costs of the System. The Commission Also Erred in
   Adopting a Generator Funding Model for The Funding of Network
   Upgrades for Co-Located Load with No Supporting Evidence. See
   Florida Gas, 604 F.3d at 639 (“[T]he Commission ‘must be able to
   demonstrate that it has made a reasoned decision based upon substantial
   evidence in the record.’”) (citation omitted); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y.,
   305 U.S. at 229 (explaining that substantial evidence means “more than a
   mere scintilla”); see also 5 U.S.C. § 706.

       i. FERC’s order is arbitrary and capricious in abandoning the
          main construct of service to load, which is that customers share
          in the embedded costs of the system. See State Farm, 463 U.S. at
          43; Coal. of MISO Transmission Customers, 45 F.4th at 1009
          (quoting S.C. Pub. Serv. Auth. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 53 (D.C. Cir.
          2014) (per curiam)).

       ii. The Commission’s proposal that co-located load must self-fund
           any needed transmission upgrades is arbitrary and capricious
           because FERC has not explained its decision to depart from
           prior precedent. See F.C.C. v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556
           U.S. at 515 (“[T]he requirement that an agency provide reasoned
           explanation for its action would ordinarily demand that it display
           awareness that it is changing position. An agency may not, for
           example, depart from a prior policy sub silentio or simply disregard
           rules that are still on the books.”); New England Power Generators
           Ass’n, 881 F.3d at 211 (“Although case-by-case adjudication
           sometimes results in decisions that seem at odds but can be
           distinguished on their facts, it is the agency’s responsibility to
           provide a reasoned explanation of why those facts matter.”); W.
           Deptford Energy, LLC, 766 F.3d at 20 (“It is textbook administrative
           law that an agency must ‘provide[ ] a reasoned explanation for
           departing from precedent or treating similar situations differently,’
           and Commission cases are no exception.”) (citations omitted); Cal.
           Pub. Utils. Comm’n, 879 F.3d at 977 (“FERC departed from this
           policy without acknowledgment or explanation. This departure was
           arbitrary and capricious.”); Sw. Airlines Co., 926 F.3d at 856 (“‘A
           full and rational explanation’ becomes ‘especially important’ when,
           as here, an agency elects to ‘shift [its] policy’ or ‘depart[ ] from its
           typical manner of’ administering a program. . . . [FERC] must at
           least ‘acknowledge’ its seemingly inconsistent precedents and either

          offer a reason ‘to distinguish them’ or ‘explain its apparent rejection
         of their approach’ . . . . But however the agency justifies its new

         advantage” or from maintaining “any unreasonable difference in

     iii. The 206 Order departs from traditional cost causation
          principles and fails to explain or justify its departure. See, e.g.,
          Nat’l R.R. Passenger Corp. v. PPL Elec. Utils. Corp., 173 FERC ¶
          61,043, at PP 13–14 (2020); see also Fox Television Stations, Inc.,

          for example, depart from a prior policy sub silentio or simply

     iv. The Commission provides no record evidence nor a reasoned
         explanation for why co-located load should not be charged like
         other load, i.e., with the upgrade cost recovered as part of the
         transmission rates charged to all customers. Transmission
         owners are permitted to earn a reasonable return on the
         investments necessary to construct, operate, and maintain
         transmission facilities, including those network upgrades
         required to serve co-located load. See, e.g., Fed. Power Comm’n
         v. Hope Nat. Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591 (1944); Bluefield Water Works
         & Improvement Co. v. Pub. Service Comm’n of W. Va., 262 U.S.

d. The Commission is Wrong in Suggesting That CD Service Will
   Promote Efficiency or Change Siting.

      i. The Commission’s decision to require options for CD Service
         does not change how the study process or the regional planning
         process should work. See PJM Tariff §§ 31.1-31.3, 31.6, 32.

     ii. The Commission’s decision against the netting of behind the
         meter generation and the stated reasons for that decision cannot
         be logically reconciled with the structure it proposed for the new
         transmission services and its decision is therefore arbitrary and
         capricious. See State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43.

       e. The Commission’s Disregard of Reliability Considerations
         Underscores that the Replacement Rate is Not Just and Reasonable.
         See Constellation Mystic Power, LLC, 45 F.4th at 1035 (“The
         reasonableness of a rate is assessed in light of the FPA’s goals of promoting
         reliable service at reasonable rates and developing plentiful energy
         supplies.”); NAACP v. FPC, 425 U.S. at 669–70 (“[T]he principal purpose
         of [the FPA is] to encourage the orderly development of plentiful supplies
         of electricity . . . at reasonable prices.”).

3. FERC Exceeded Its Jurisdiction. See 16 U.S.C. § 824(b).

      a. FERC’s Replacement Rate Violates the Major Questions Doctrine. See
         West Virginia v. EPA, 597 U.S. 697, 723 (2022); Whitman v. Am. Trucking
         Ass’ns, 531 U.S. 457, 468 (2001) (“Congress, we have held, does not alter

           The FPA requires that the rates and charges of a public utility “in connection with the

and regulations affecting or pertaining to such rates or charges shall be just and reasonable.”14

complainant.”17 In other words, a respondent to a FPA section 206 complaint is not required to

make an affirmative showing that its existing rate is still just and reasonable.
